![Everyone's Name on Every Paper](./cover.png)

[Brian Ripley](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/),
[my doctoral supervisor](../brian-ripley-rousseeuw-prize/), published far fewer papers
than his influence would suggest. He was among R core's most active committers for two
decades, and none of that work is a paper. He used to say code mattered more than
citations — writing code debugs your thinking.

There is a second reason to distrust the counts, and it has nothing to do with what
they leave out. A paper count and a citation count are both totals over whoever is
named on the paper. Nobody measures the work; they measure the author list. So adding
names moves both numbers, without anyone writing a line more.

## Adding names multiplies papers by n, citations by more

The cheapest way to see the effect is to strip it down to arithmetic. Imagine a group
of researchers who have each already written one paper alone. They agree to put every
name on every paper. No new research gets done and no sentence is rewritten — the
papers themselves are exactly what they were. Only the author lists change.

Take $n$ researchers with one solo paper each, drawing $c_i$ citations, who put all
$n$ names on every paper. No new work exists, yet every paper count goes 1 → $n$ and
every citation count $c_i$ → $S = \sum_j c_j$:

$$\frac{S}{c_i} = n \cdot \frac{\bar{c}}{c_i}.$$

Papers multiply by exactly $n$. Citations multiply by more than $n$, and the reason is
the shape of citation counts. A handful of papers get cited enormously while most get
cited barely at all — a **heavy tail** — so the average paper in a field is cited far
more often than the typical one. That gap is what pushes $\bar{c}/c_i$ above one for
most of the group.

## Simulated citations, because the tail decides

To see how much more, we need citation counts to work with. The ones used here are made
up rather than pulled from a real database, and that is deliberate. The question is
counterfactual: it asks what the same researchers' numbers would look like both with
and without the arrangement. No real dataset holds both branches, because a group
either did it or did not. Simulating gives us the pair.

The counts are drawn from a **lognormal** distribution ($\mu = 1.5$, $\sigma = 1.2$ on
the log scale) — one whose logarithm is a bell curve, which is the usual stand-in for a
quantity with a long right tail. The median sits near 4.5 citations, with a few papers
running into the hundreds. That stands in for one field's citations. What rides on the
answer is a hiring panel's read of a CV.

::: {#multipliers .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

RNG = np.random.default_rng(0)
MU, SIGMA = 1.5, 1.2          # lognormal, on the log scale
GROUPS = (5, 10, 20)
REPS = 20_000                 # many draws, so the medians are not a fluke of one

print(f"{'n':>3}  {'papers':>7}  {'median':>9}  {'share above':>12}  {'large-n':>8}")
print(f"{'':>3}  {'':>7}  {'citations':>9}  {'n times':>12}  {'limit':>8}")
for n in GROUPS:
    c = RNG.lognormal(MU, SIGMA, size=(REPS, n))
    # Everyone is credited with the group total, so the multiplier is S / c_i.
    mult = c.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) / c
    limit = n * np.exp(SIGMA**2 / 2)   # what median(S / c_i) tends to as n grows
    print(f"{n:>3}  {n:>6}x  {np.median(mult):>8.1f}x  {np.mean(mult > n):>11.0%}"
          f"  {limit:>7.1f}x")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
  n   papers     median   share above   large-n
              citations       n times     limit
  5       5x       7.3x          63%     10.3x
 10      10x      17.2x          67%     20.5x
 20      20x      37.3x          70%     41.1x
```
:::
:::


The median beats $n\times$ at every size — 7.3× at $n = 5$, 37× at $n = 20$. The
"share above n times" column gives the fraction of researchers who do better than the
$n\times$ their paper count grew by, and at every size it is most of them. But a
median hides who pays for that.

## The gain is unequal, making it a transaction

Everyone ends on the same total $S$, whatever they brought. That is the whole of it:
the group's citations are pooled, then handed to each member in full. Someone who
arrived with a lightly cited paper walks away with the group total — and so does the
person who arrived with the most cited paper in the room.

The plot below draws that swap for one draw at each group size. Each row is one
researcher. The left end of their line is what they earned alone, and the right end is
what they are credited with afterwards.

::: {#cell-fig-inflation .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SOLO, COMBINED, REF = "#6b7280", "#4a3aa7", "#eb6834"
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7.4, 8.2), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": GROUPS, "hspace": 0.16})

for ax, n in zip(axes, GROUPS):
    c = np.sort(rng.lognormal(MU, SIGMA, size=n))
    total, y = c.sum(), np.arange(n)
    ax.hlines(y, c, total, color=SOLO, lw=1.2, alpha=0.55, zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(c, y, s=34, color=SOLO, zorder=3, label="solo: own paper only")
    ax.scatter(np.full(n, total), y, s=34, color=COMBINED, zorder=3,
               label="combined: credited the group total")
    ax.scatter(n * c, y, s=52, marker="|", color=REF, lw=1.8, zorder=4,
               label=r"$n \times$ the solo count")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.9, n - 0.1)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_ylabel(f"$n = {n}$", fontsize=11)
    ax.grid(axis="x", color="0.9", lw=0.7)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    for side in ("top", "right", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
for ax in axes[:-1]:
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", bottom=False)

axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper left",
               bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.6))
axes[-1].set_xlabel("credited citations (log scale)", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![One draw per group size. Left ends are what each researcher earned alone; right ends are what all of them are credited with after combining. The orange tick marks n times the solo count: left of the total, that researcher beat n times; right of it, they did worse.](index_files/figure-html/fig-inflation-output-1.png){#fig-inflation}
:::
:::


Across the 20,000 draws above, two thirds of researchers clear $n\times$. The most
cited member of a group never can. A total is at most $n$ times the largest number in
it ($S \le n\,c_{\max}$), so whoever holds that largest count still gains, but by less
than the $n\times$ their paper count grew by.

That is the cost, and it is a relative one. Nobody's citation count falls. The most
cited member simply gains least, and everyone else closes the distance on them. Their
standing is what the arrangement spends, which is why that person has to be given some
reason to agree.

## Real publishing runs the same sum

None of this stays inside the simulation. The same sum — pool the credit, then hand the
total to everyone named — runs in real publishing at three different scales. What the
strong party gets paid with is different at each one. The arithmetic does not change,
only the currency.

Among authors, the currency is seniority. A 2024
[meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-54909-w) put honorary authorship in
health sciences at 26% when researchers were simply asked. It fell to 18% when they
were first shown the ICMJE criteria for who counts as an author, and rose to 51% when
their declared contributions were checked against those criteria.

Among journals, the currency is reciprocity: you cite me, I cite you. By 2019 the
Journal Citation Reports had suspended 46 journal pairs — 55 journals in all — for
trading citations within the pair at a level the index treats as excessive.
[CIDRE](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-93572-3) is one method for spotting such
groups from the flow of citations between journals.

Among institutions, the currency is cash. In 2011
[*Science*](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.334.6061.1344) reported that more than 60
highly cited researchers had added King Abdulaziz University as a paid second
affiliation. By 2014 the university ranked second worldwide on the highly cited list.

## Caveat: the temptation needs no conspiracy

No arrangement is needed to feel this pull. Teams genuinely do produce more-cited work
than solo authors — [Wuchty, Jones and Uzzi](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1136099)
found as much across 19.9 million papers. So the honest incentive and the dishonest one
point the same way: add names. Most author lists are exactly what they look like, and
none of the cases above is the model running at full strength.

But the arithmetic cannot tell an earned name from a gifted one. Neither can the counts
built on top of it. Ripley's could not see him.
